criteria_results.title: Title VII damages instruction does NOT disclose the $200,000 statutory cap to the jury
criteria_results.reasoning: The instructions do not disclose the $200,000 statutory cap to the jury. Instruction No. 11 explicitly states 'Do not mention the § 1981a(b)(3) cap ... to the jury; § 1981a(c)(2) forbids it,' but this is in a drafting note marked for deletion before filing, not in the jury-facing instruction text itself. The actual instruction text given to the jury contains no mention of any dollar cap or statutory ceiling. The punitive damages instruction (No. 16) and the damages general instruction (No. 11) both omit any reference to the $200,000 cap. The criterion is satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains that Title VII damages cap is not disclosed to jury
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo explicitly addresses the Title VII statutory damages cap in section 3.8 (Damages, punitive damages, and remedies). It states: 'The jury may not be told (§ 1981a(c)(2)).' This directly explains that the cap is not disclosed to the jury, citing the statutory provision that prohibits informing the jury of the cap. The memo also notes that Creston falls in the 201-500 employee tier with a $200,000 combined cap, and that the verdict form structure is what protects the cap post-verdict.

criteria_results.title: No Faragher/Ellerth instruction included for the retaliation claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output explicitly states in the Preliminary Statement: 'Consistent with the Order, Defendant does not propose an instruction on the Faragher/Ellerth affirmative defense. Order § V.A.' No Faragher/Ellerth instruction appears anywhere in the proposed jury instructions. The instructions address Title VII retaliation elements, but-for causation, timing, legitimate business reason, cat's paw, and punitive damages (with Kolstad good-faith defense), but no Faragher/Ellerth affirmative defense instruction is included.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies defendant's Faragher/Ellerth request for retaliation claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo explicitly identifies that the defendant's pretrial brief (Brief No. 2) requested a Faragher/Ellerth instruction for the retaliation claim. Section 3.1 is titled 'Faragher/Ellerth (Brief § II) --- withdraw' and discusses how the Brief requested this instruction and why it should be withdrawn. The summary table also lists 'Brief No. 2 --- Faragher/Ellerth' as an item to withdraw.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains legal basis for excluding Faragher/Ellerth from retaliation
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo's section 3.1 on Faragher/Ellerth states that 'The defense also does not fit on the merits. It applies to supervisor harassment where no tangible employment action was taken, and a termination is a tangible employment action.' This explains that Faragher/Ellerth applies to harassment (hostile work environment) cases, not retaliation cases, and specifically notes the tangible employment action distinction. However, the primary reason given for withdrawal is the Court's order language, not the legal distinction between harassment and retaliation defenses. The memo does explain that the defense 'applies to supervisor harassment where no tangible employment action was taken' — this is the legal basis distinguishing it from retaliation cases. The criterion asks whether the memo explains that Faragher/Ellerth is an affirmative defense to vicarious liability in hostile-work-environment harassment cases, not retaliation cases. The memo does make this distinction, stating it 'applies to supervisor harassment where no tangible employment action was taken.' This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Title VII retaliation instruction uses but-for causation standard
criteria_results.reasoning: Proposed Instruction No. 3 explicitly defines but-for causation for the Title VII claim, stating Plaintiff must prove 'that Creston would not have terminated her employment in the absence of that complaint.' It cites Nassar, 570 U.S. 338 (2013), and expressly distinguishes the but-for standard from the contributing-factor standard used for the Ohio Whistleblower claim. The instruction also states 'It is not enough for Plaintiff to prove that her complaint was a motivating factor, a contributing factor, or one of several things Creston considered.' The verdict form Question 1 also uses the but-for formulation. The instruction clearly and correctly applies the Nassar but-for causation standard to the Title VII retaliation claim.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower instruction uses contributing-factor causation standard
criteria_results.reasoning: The Ohio Whistleblower instruction (Proposed Instruction No. 9) explicitly uses a 'contributing factor' causation standard, defining it as 'a factor that actually played a part in the decision.' The instruction also explicitly distinguishes this from the but-for standard used for the Title VII claim, stating 'This standard is different from, and less demanding than, the but-for standard that applies to Plaintiff's Title VII claim.' The verdict form (Question 9) also uses the contributing factor language. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains different causation standards for the two retaliation claims
criteria_results.reasoning: The memo discusses both causation standards. In section 3.5, it explicitly addresses the distinction between the but-for standard (Title VII, Brief No. 6) and the contributing-factor standard (WPA/Ohio Whistleblower, Brief No. 7/No. 9). The summary table also references 'but-for causation' and 'contributing factor' as separate instructions. The memo notes that the contributing-factor definition in the Brief 'comes from federal whistleblower statutes and is the most favorable to Plaintiff' and proposes replacing it with an 'actually played a part' definition. It also references limiting instructions (Nos. 2 and 7) to prevent the jury from applying a blended standard. However, the memo does not explicitly cite University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center v. Nassar (2013) by name for the but-for standard. That said, the criterion says 'citing or referencing Nassar' — the memo references the but-for standard for Title VII retaliation and the contributing-factor standard for the Ohio WPA claim, which satisfies the substance of the criterion even without a Nassar citation. The criterion is met because the memo clearly discusses the distinction between the two causation standards applicable to the two retaliation claims.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies plaintiff's mixed-motive request as legally incorrect
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo discusses the but-for causation standard for Title VII retaliation (Brief No. 6) and notes it should be kept with additions including the 'Bostock need not be sole cause sentence and the contrast with the WPA standard.' However, the memo never specifically identifies that plaintiff's pretrial brief requested a mixed-motive instruction for the Title VII retaliation claim, nor does it explain that this is legally incorrect under University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center v. Nassar, which requires but-for causation for retaliation claims (as opposed to the motivating factor standard for status-based discrimination). The memo focuses on correcting Creston's own proposed instructions, not on identifying and rejecting a mixed-motive instruction requested by the plaintiff. The criterion specifically requires the memo to identify plaintiff's mixed-motive request as legally incorrect under Nassar. This is not addressed.

criteria_results.title: After-acquired evidence instruction is included
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output includes Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 14, titled 'After-Acquired Evidence,' which specifically addresses Okafor-Reyes's alleged misrepresentation of her MBA credentials on her 2016 employment application. The instruction explains that this is not a defense to liability but may limit lost wages recovery, sets out the two-part McKennon test, and is incorporated into the special verdict form as Questions 4 and 12.

criteria_results.title: After-acquired evidence instruction frames doctrine as remedies limitation, not complete defense
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 14 explicitly states: 'This contention, if proved, is not a defense to liability on any of Plaintiff's claims and has no bearing on whether Creston retaliated against Plaintiff or breached a contract with her.' It then explains that the doctrine 'may, however, limit the lost wages and benefits Plaintiff may recover,' and specifically that if proved, 'Plaintiff may not recover lost wages or benefits for any period after [DATE], the date on which Creston learned of the misrepresentation.' The drafting note also explicitly corrects the prior brief's error: 'Pretrial Brief No. 3, which asked the Court to tell the jury that after-acquired evidence is a complete defense to all claims and cited McKennon for that proposition. McKennon holds the opposite: it is not a bar to liability and limits only remedies.' This is fully consistent with McKennon v. Nashville Banner Publishing Co., 513 U.S. 352 (1995).

criteria_results.title: Cover memo explains after-acquired evidence is remedies limitation per McKennon
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo explicitly discusses McKennon v. Nashville Banner, 513 U.S. 352 (1995) in section 3.2, stating that the doctrine does not bar liability but only limits remedies. It explains that if the employer proves the wrongdoing 'was of such severity that the employee in fact would have been terminated on those grounds alone if the employer had known of it,' then reinstatement and front pay are unavailable and back pay runs only to the date of discovery. The memo also criticizes the Pretrial Brief for citing McKennon 'for the opposite rule' and recommends replacing the erroneous instruction with a proper McKennon remedy-limitation instruction.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo notes defendant's overbroad framing of after-acquired evidence as complete defense
criteria_results.reasoning: Section 3.2 of the memo explicitly addresses the after-acquired evidence issue, stating that 'McKennon v. Nashville Banner, 513 U.S. 352 (1995), holds that after-acquired evidence of wrongdoing does not bar liability' and that 'The Brief cites McKennon for the opposite rule.' The summary table (Brief No. 3) also notes the brief 'Calls it a complete defense to all claims' and recommends replacing it with a McKennon remedy-limitation instruction. This directly identifies the defendant's overbroad framing and explains why it is legally incorrect.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower instruction addresses internal-reporting prerequisite under ORC § 4113.52
criteria_results.reasoning: Proposed Instruction No. 8 is entirely dedicated to the Ohio Whistleblower Protection Act's internal-reporting requirement under ORC § 4113.52. It sets out three elements the plaintiff must prove: (1) oral notification to a supervisor or responsible officer before filing externally; (2) subsequent written report with sufficient detail; and (3) that Creston did not correct or make a reasonable and good-faith effort to correct the violation within 24 hours. The instruction also directs the jury that failure to prove any one of these three requirements means a verdict for Creston on the Ohio Whistleblower claim. The special verdict form (Question 8) mirrors these requirements. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Internal-reporting instruction treats verbal report as disputed factual issue for jury
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 8 explicitly states: 'Plaintiff contends that she orally reported her concern to Plant Manager Greg Felton on February 28, 2023. Creston disputes that any such report was made. It is for you to decide, based on all of the evidence and the instructions I have given you on evaluating the credibility of witnesses, whether Plaintiff has proved that she made the oral notification.' This clearly frames the verbal report as a contested factual issue for the jury to resolve, satisfying the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction references at-will disclaimer from Employee Handbook
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 10 (Count IV — Breach of Implied Employment Contract) explicitly references the at-will disclaimer from page 3 of the Employee Handbook, quoting it: 'the at-will provision on page 3 of the Handbook, which states that "[n]othing in this handbook creates a contract of employment," that employment "may be terminated by either party at any time, for any lawful reason, with or without cause," and that no one other than the Chief Executive Officer, in a signed writing, may make a contrary agreement.' This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction references progressive-discipline provision from Employee Handbook
criteria_results.reasoning: Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 10 (Count IV — Breach of Implied Employment Contract) explicitly references the progressive-discipline provision from pages 27 and 28 of Creston's Employee Handbook multiple times. It states that Plaintiff claims Creston breached an implied contract 'by terminating her without following the progressive-discipline procedure described on pages 27 and 28 of Creston's Employee Handbook.' It also references the Handbook's statement on page 28 that Creston 'reserves the right to determine the appropriate level of discipline in each individual situation' and that steps 'may be repeated, combined, or skipped.' The special verdict form (Questions 13-15) also references the progressive-discipline provision. The criterion is clearly satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction presents conflict between disclaimer and progressive discipline for jury determination
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 10 on breach of implied employment contract explicitly frames the tension between the at-will disclaimer and the progressive-discipline provision as a factual question for the jury. It lists multiple factors for the jury to weigh in deciding 'the first question' (mutual intent), including the at-will disclaimer language, its clarity and conspicuousness, the handbook's reservation of rights, and whether Plaintiff actually relied on the progressive-discipline provision. The instruction states 'you should consider the Handbook as a whole and all of the circumstances' and does not resolve the conflict as a matter of law. The special verdict form (Questions 13-14) similarly submits these as jury questions. The drafting note even acknowledges that the prior brief's approach of directing a defense verdict based on the disclaimer was rejected by the Court, and the instruction was revised to present a multi-factor jury question. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract instruction reflects Ohio law (Mers v. Dispatch Printing Co.)
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 10 explicitly cites Mers v. Dispatch Printing Co., 19 Ohio St. 3d 100 (1985) and its progeny, and frames the implied-contract question as a multi-factor jury inquiry rather than directing a defense verdict based solely on the at-will disclaimer. It instructs the jury to consider the handbook as a whole, the specificity of the progressive-discipline language, the disclaimer language, the reservation-of-rights clause, and whether Plaintiff actually relied on the provision—consistent with Mers's totality-of-circumstances approach. The instruction does not state that an at-will disclaimer automatically negates an implied contract claim; instead it treats the disclaimer as one factor among several. The drafting note even explicitly flags that the prior brief's approach (directing a verdict if the disclaimer was 'clear and conspicuous') was inconsistent with the Order's reading of Karnes and Mers. This is fully consistent with Ohio law recognizing that handbook provisions can create implied contractual obligations under certain circumstances.

criteria_results.title: Mitigation instruction is included
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output includes Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 13, titled 'Mitigation of Damages,' which is a detailed failure-to-mitigate instruction covering the burden of proof, the definition of substantially equivalent employment, and the effect on damages. The verdict form also includes mitigation questions (Questions 3 and 11). The criterion is clearly satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Mitigation instruction places burden of proof on defendant
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 13 (Mitigation of Damages) explicitly states: 'Creston has the burden of proving by a preponderance of the evidence that Plaintiff failed to mitigate her damages.' The burden is correctly placed on the defendant, not the plaintiff. The drafting note also confirms this, noting that the prior brief incorrectly placed the burden on Plaintiff and that doing so would be contrary to settled Sixth Circuit law (Rasimas) and reversible error.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo notes correction of mitigation burden from defendant's brief
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo explicitly addresses the mitigation burden issue in Section 3.3, stating that 'Brief No. 4 places the burden on Plaintiff. That is legal error and should be corrected.' It cites both Rasimas v. Mich. Dep't of Mental Health, 714 F.2d 614, 623-24 (6th Cir. 1983) and Ford Motor Co. v. EEOC, 458 U.S. 219, 231-32 (1982), explaining that under Sixth Circuit law the employer bears the burden of proving failure to mitigate. The memo also appears in the summary table (Brief No. 4) noting 'Puts the burden on Plaintiff. Under Sixth Circuit law (Rasimas) the burden is on the employer.' This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Temporal proximity / circumstantial evidence instruction included for retaliation
criteria_results.reasoning: Proposed Instruction No. 4 ('Count I --- Timing of Events') directly addresses temporal proximity as a form of circumstantial evidence the jury may consider in evaluating causation/retaliatory motive. It explains that a short interval between protected activity and an adverse action may, together with other evidence, support an inference of causation, and that a longer interval may weaken that inference. The instruction also notes that timing alone is insufficient. The drafting note references the Cavender email and the Court's characterization of Exhibit 14 as 'bridg[ing] the temporal gap,' showing awareness of the specific timeline. While the instruction does not explicitly cite the March 22, 2023 Cavender email (13 days after EPA complaint) or the August 3, 2023 termination date (approximately 5 months after EPA complaint) by name in the instruction text itself, it provides general guidance on temporal proximity as circumstantial evidence and the drafting notes acknowledge these specific dates. The criterion requires that the instructions 'address temporal proximity as a form of circumstantial evidence the jury may consider in evaluating retaliatory motive, referencing or accounting for the timeline.' Instruction No. 4 satisfies the first part (addressing temporal proximity as circumstantial evidence), and the drafting notes account for the timeline. The instruction text itself does not explicitly reference the specific dates, but it does provide the framework for the jury to consider timing. This satisfies the criterion as stated.

criteria_results.title: Temporal proximity instruction permits inference of retaliatory motive
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 4 (Count I — Timing of Events) explicitly states: 'A short interval between protected activity and an adverse action may, together with other evidence, support an inference of causation.' This directly permits the jury to consider close temporal proximity as evidence of retaliatory motive. The instruction does not direct the jury to disregard timing; rather, it treats timing as one circumstance to weigh with all other evidence. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Temporal proximity instruction does not mandate finding of retaliation
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 4 (Count I — Timing of Events) explicitly states: 'A short interval between protected activity and an adverse action may, together with other evidence, support an inference of causation' and 'The fact that an adverse action followed protected activity does not, by itself, prove that the protected activity caused the adverse action. You must decide causation on the basis of all of the evidence.' This language clearly does not mandate a finding of retaliation based on temporal proximity alone; it treats timing as one factor among many and expressly disclaims that timing alone is sufficient.

criteria_results.title: Kolstad good-faith defense instruction included for punitive damages
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 16 explicitly includes the Kolstad good-faith defense. It states that even if Plaintiff proves a managerial employee acted with malice or reckless indifference, Creston may avoid punitive damages by proving it made good-faith efforts to comply with Title VII and that the managerial employee's conduct was contrary to those efforts. The instruction cites Kolstad v. Am. Dental Ass'n, 527 U.S. 526 (1999) as authority and details the factors the jury may consider in evaluating good-faith compliance. The special verdict form (Questions 5-7) also implements this defense structurally. The criterion is fully satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Kolstad defense is distinguished from Faragher/Ellerth in the instructions or memo
criteria_results.reasoning: The memorandum explicitly and clearly distinguishes Kolstad from Faragher/Ellerth. In Section 3.1, it explains that Faragher/Ellerth applies to 'supervisor harassment where no tangible employment action was taken' and has 'no application to the Title VII retaliation claim' per the Court's order. It then notes that the same policy evidence 'is properly presented under Kolstad (No. 16), which the Order expressly invited.' In Section 3.8, it further discusses Kolstad as the proper vehicle for punitive damages, distinct from the Faragher/Ellerth defense. The memo recommends withdrawing the Faragher/Ellerth instruction entirely while keeping and restructuring the Kolstad instruction. The two doctrines are treated as distinct: Faragher/Ellerth as a vicarious liability defense inapplicable to retaliation, and Kolstad as a good-faith defense relevant to punitive damages. This distinction is clearly and explicitly addressed.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form (not general verdict) is included
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output includes a detailed Special Verdict Form with specific interrogatories organized by claim (Part I - Title VII, Part II - Ohio Whistleblower, Part III - Implied Contract). Each part contains numbered questions requiring specific factual findings (e.g., causation, damages amounts, mitigation, after-acquired evidence, punitive damages eligibility) rather than a simple general verdict. This is clearly a special verdict form with interrogatories, not a general verdict form.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form has separate interrogatories for Title VII retaliation claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The special verdict form includes a dedicated PART I — COUNT I: TITLE VII RETALIATION section with separate interrogatories (Questions 1–7) specifically addressing the Title VII retaliation claim, covering causation, damages, mitigation, after-acquired evidence, and punitive damages. These are clearly separated from the Ohio Whistleblower (Part II) and implied contract (Part III) sections.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form has separate interrogatories for Ohio Whistleblower claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The special verdict form in Part II (COUNT II: OHIO WHISTLEBLOWER PROTECTION ACT) contains separate interrogatories specifically for the Ohio Whistleblower Protection Act claim, including Questions 8 through 12, which address the internal-reporting requirement, contributing-factor causation, damages, mitigation, and after-acquired evidence for that claim separately from the Title VII and implied contract claims.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form has separate interrogatories for implied employment contract claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The special verdict form includes Part III — Count IV: Breach of Implied Contract, which contains three separate interrogatories (Questions 13, 14, and 15) specifically addressing the breach of implied employment contract claim. Question 13 asks about mutual intent to be bound by the progressive-discipline provision, Question 14 asks whether the provision applied to a RIF termination, and Question 15 asks for economic damages. These are clearly separate interrogatories dedicated to the implied contract claim.

criteria_results.title: Title VII retaliation damages instruction includes compensatory and punitive damages
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output includes Instruction No. 11 (Damages — General Principles), Instruction No. 12 (Lost Wages and Benefits/Back Pay), Instruction No. 15 (Compensatory Damages — Emotional Distress), and Instruction No. 16 (Punitive Damages — Title VII Claim Only; Good-Faith Compliance). Instruction No. 15 explicitly addresses compensatory damages (emotional distress, medical expenses) for the Title VII claim. Instruction No. 16 explicitly addresses punitive damages for the Title VII claim, including the malice/reckless indifference standard and the Kolstad good-faith defense. The special verdict form (Questions 2, 5, 6, 7) also separately addresses compensatory damages and punitive damages for the Title VII claim. Both categories are clearly addressed.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower damages instruction is differentiated from Title VII damages
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output clearly differentiates Ohio Whistleblower damages from Title VII damages in several ways: (1) Instruction No. 11 (Damages General) explicitly states that 'Damages for emotional distress and punitive damages are not recoverable on Plaintiff's breach-of-contract claim,' and Instruction No. 16 states punitive damages apply to 'Title VII Claim Only' and explicitly says 'You may not award punitive damages on the Ohio Whistleblower claim or the breach-of-contract claim.' (2) Instruction No. 15 on emotional distress includes a bracketed note '[or her Ohio Whistleblower claim]' with a drafting note to 'Confirm whether emotional-distress damages are recoverable under R.C. 4113.52(E) before including the bracketed Count II reference,' showing awareness of the distinction. (3) The verdict form treats the two claims separately with different questions (Part I for Title VII, Part II for Ohio Whistleblower), and the Ohio Whistleblower section brackets the emotional distress line item (Question 10(b)) indicating uncertainty about its availability. (4) The punitive damages question (Questions 5-7) appears only in Part I (Title VII), not in Part II (Ohio Whistleblower). These distinctions clearly differentiate the damages provisions between the two claims rather than treating them identically.

criteria_results.title: Implied-contract damages instruction reflects contract damages measure
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 11 (Damages — General Principles) explicitly states: 'Damages for emotional distress and punitive damages are not recoverable on Plaintiff's breach-of-contract claim.' The special verdict form for Count IV (Question 15) asks only for 'economic damages' caused by Creston's failure to follow the progressive-discipline provision, which aligns with a contract/expectation damages measure. No punitive damages or emotional distress categories appear in the contract claim's verdict questions. The instructions clearly differentiate the contract claim's damages from the Title VII claim's damages categories.

criteria_results.title: Pre-existing condition / eggshell plaintiff instruction included for emotional distress
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 15 explicitly addresses the pre-existing anxiety condition (treatment beginning 2020) in the context of emotional distress damages. It states that Plaintiff may not recover for the pre-existing condition itself, but may recover for aggravation caused by Creston's unlawful conduct. It also includes the eggshell plaintiff principle: 'If you find that Plaintiff was more susceptible to emotional harm because of a pre-existing condition, you may award damages for the full extent of the aggravation that Creston's unlawful conduct actually caused, even if a person without that condition would have suffered less harm; but you may not award damages for the pre-existing condition itself.' This satisfies both prongs of the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Preliminary instructions on role of jury included
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output does not include a preliminary instruction on the role and duties of the jury (e.g., deciding facts, following the law as instructed by the court). The Preliminary Statement explicitly defers this: 'Defendant requests that the Court give its customary general instructions (duties of the jury, evidence, credibility of witnesses, expert testimony, corporate parties, and deliberations).' The proposed instructions begin with Instruction No. 1 on burden of proof, which touches on procedural matters but does not address the jury's role in deciding facts versus the court's role in deciding law, or other standard preliminary jury role instructions. No instruction explaining that the jury decides facts, must follow the law as given by the court, etc., is included in the set.

criteria_results.title: Preliminary instruction on burden of proof included
criteria_results.reasoning: Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 1 is explicitly titled 'Burden of Proof --- Preponderance of the Evidence; Separate Consideration of Each Claim' and clearly states that Plaintiff bears the burden of proving each element of each claim by a preponderance of the evidence, defining that standard as proving something is more likely true than not true. This satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Standard witness credibility instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output does not include a standalone witness credibility instruction advising the jury on how to evaluate witness testimony (e.g., considering demeanor, interest, bias, consistency, corroboration). The Preliminary Statement notes that Defendant requests the Court give its 'customary general instructions (duties of the jury, evidence, credibility of witnesses, expert testimony, corporate parties, and deliberations),' but this is merely a request that the Court provide its own standard instructions — it is not itself a proposed credibility instruction. No proposed instruction in the set (Nos. 1–16) addresses witness credibility factors. Instruction No. 8 briefly mentions 'the instructions I have given you on evaluating the credibility of witnesses,' which presupposes such an instruction exists but does not constitute one. The criterion requires that the instruction set include a standard witness credibility instruction, which it does not.

criteria_results.title: Title VII retaliation elements instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 2 explicitly lists the three elements for the Title VII retaliation claim: (1) Plaintiff engaged in activity protected by Title VII; (2) Creston took a materially adverse action against Plaintiff; and (3) Plaintiff's protected activity was the but-for cause of Creston's decision to terminate her employment. This satisfies all three required elements including the but-for causation standard, which is further elaborated in Instruction No. 3.

criteria_results.title: Ohio Whistleblower elements instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output includes Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 7 ('Count II — Ohio Whistleblower Protection Act: Elements'), which lists the three elements Plaintiff must prove: (1) compliance with the internal-reporting requirements of ORC § 4113.52 before filing the EPA complaint, (2) an adverse employment action, and (3) that the EPA complaint was a contributing factor in the termination. It also includes Instruction No. 8 ('Count II — Internal-Reporting Requirement'), which details the specific internal-reporting prerequisites (oral notification, written report, and employer's failure to correct within 24 hours). Both instructions together clearly satisfy the criterion of listing the elements including the internal-reporting prerequisite and the protected whistleblowing activity.

criteria_results.title: Implied employment contract elements instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 10 (Count IV — Breach of Implied Employment Contract) provides a substantive instruction on the elements of the implied contract claim. It covers: (1) mutual intent that the handbook provision was a binding term limiting termination rights; (2) whether the progressive-discipline provision applied to the termination at issue (RIF); and (3) whether Creston failed to comply and Plaintiff suffered damages. It also addresses the at-will presumption, the multi-factor Mers analysis, handbook disclaimers, and the scope of the provision. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Legitimate non-retaliatory reason (RIF) instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 5 ('Legitimate Business Reason; Reduction in Force; Business Judgment') directly addresses the RIF as the asserted legitimate, non-retaliatory reason for termination. It explains that Creston contends the termination was due to a company-wide reduction in force for financial reasons, that Creston does not bear the burden of proving its stated reason was the actual reason, and that if the jury finds the stated reason is not the true reason it may (but is not required to) infer retaliation. It also instructs that an employer is entitled to make business decisions including eliminating positions for any lawful reason. This squarely covers the legitimate-reason/pretext framework the criterion requires.

criteria_results.title: Protected activity instruction uses reasonable good-faith belief standard
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output addresses protected activity in Instruction No. 2 (Count I — Title VII Retaliation: Elements). However, the instruction states that the Court has 'already determined that Plaintiff's January 17, 2023 internal complaint of sex-based pay discrimination was protected activity under Title VII,' and instructs the jury to treat the first two elements (protected activity and materially adverse action) as established. Because the Court has already resolved the protected activity question as a matter of law, the instruction does not ask the jury to find whether actual discrimination occurred — but it also does not instruct the jury on the reasonable good-faith belief standard. The instruction simply removes the protected activity element from jury consideration entirely. The criterion requires that the instruction tell the jury that the plaintiff need only have had a reasonable, good-faith belief that she was opposing unlawful discrimination — not that actual discrimination occurred. Since the instruction bypasses this standard entirely (by treating the element as established) rather than affirmatively stating the reasonable good-faith belief standard, it does not satisfy the criterion as described. The criterion is specifically about what standard the instruction uses for protected activity, and the instruction uses no standard at all for that element — it is simply removed from jury consideration. This means the instruction neither correctly states the reasonable good-faith belief standard nor incorrectly requires actual discrimination; it omits the standard altogether. Given that the criterion asks whether the instruction 'instructs that the plaintiff need only have had a reasonable, good-faith belief,' and the instruction does not include this language, the criterion is not satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Citations to Sixth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions included
criteria_results.reasoning: The criterion requires citations to Sixth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions (Civil) where applicable. The document explicitly acknowledges in the Preliminary Statement that 'The Sixth Circuit has not promulgated pattern civil jury instructions.' Accordingly, no Sixth Circuit Pattern Jury Instructions are cited anywhere in the document. Instead, the agent cites Seventh Circuit and Eleventh Circuit pattern instructions, OJI-CV (Ohio Jury Instructions Civil), and case law. Since the criterion requires that at least some instructions reference specific Sixth Circuit Pattern Jury Instruction numbers or titles, and none appear anywhere in the document, the output fails this criterion.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo lists each instruction with its legal basis
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo discusses the proposed instructions extensively and provides numerous legal citations (McKennon, Rasimas, Ford Motor Co., Contreras, Mers, Karnes, Mickey, Staub, Kolstad, Bostock, R.C. 4113.52, 42 U.S.C. § 1981a, etc.) throughout its analysis. However, the criterion requires that the memo identify each proposed instruction (or groups of related instructions) and pair each with a specific legal basis. The memo does contain a summary table (Section 2) that lists Brief numbers and new instruction numbers, and the narrative sections discuss legal authority for various instructions. But the memo does not systematically list each of the 16 proposed instructions (Nos. 1–16) with their corresponding legal basis in a clear, instruction-by-instruction pairing. The table in Section 2 covers only the instructions that are changes from the Brief (Nos. 2–10 and some new ones), and does not address all 16 instructions with their legal bases. Instructions like No. 1 (preliminary/general damages), No. 5 (business judgment), No. 6 (cat's paw), No. 11 (general damages), No. 12 (back pay), etc. are mentioned only briefly without systematic legal authority pairing. The memo is more of a strategic analysis than a systematic instruction-by-instruction legal basis document. That said, the summary table does pair most changed instructions with their issues and recommendations including legal references, and the narrative provides substantial legal authority for the major instructions. The criterion asks for identification of each instruction with its legal basis — the memo does this for most but not all instructions in a systematic way, and the new instructions (Nos. 1, 5, 6, 11, 12) lack explicit legal basis citations in the table or elsewhere. This is a close call, but the memo does substantially identify instructions and pair them with legal authority for the majority, even if not perfectly systematic for every single one of the 16 instructions.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies rejected instruction requests with reasoning
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo clearly identifies multiple rejected/withdrawn instruction requests with detailed legal reasoning. For example: (1) Brief No. 2 (Faragher/Ellerth) is recommended for withdrawal because the Court's order explicitly stated it 'has no application to the Title VII retaliation claim' and the Court 'will not entertain' such an instruction, and because the defense doesn't apply to tangible employment actions like termination. (2) Brief No. 3 (after-acquired evidence as complete defense) is rejected because McKennon v. Nashville Banner holds it does not bar liability but only limits remedies, and the Brief cited McKennon for the opposite rule. (3) Brief No. 4 (mitigation with burden on plaintiff) is rejected because Sixth Circuit law under Rasimas places the burden on the employer. (4) Brief No. 5 (WPA prerequisites) is rejected because it omits the statutory written-report requirement. These are well beyond the minimum two rejected instructions with legal reasoning required by the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Cover memo identifies areas requiring particular legal care
criteria_results.reasoning: The cover memo extensively identifies specific legal issues requiring careful drafting. It names numerous specific doctrines and standards: (1) the Faragher/Ellerth defense and its inapplicability to retaliation claims; (2) after-acquired evidence under McKennon and the correct 'would have terminated' test vs. the wrong 'effect on hiring' test; (3) mitigation burden allocation under Rasimas (burden on employer, not plaintiff); (4) Ohio WPA written-report prerequisite under R.C. 4113.52(A)(1)(a); (5) different causation standards for Title VII (but-for) vs. WPA (contributing factor); (6) Kolstad punitive damages defense requirements; (7) implied contract analysis under Mers; (8) the statutory damages cap under 42 U.S.C. § 1981a(b)(3); and more. This far exceeds the minimum threshold of two specific legal issues named with specific doctrines or standards involved.

criteria_results.title: Instructions organized by claim as required by standing order
criteria_results.reasoning: The instructions are clearly organized by claim. Count I (Title VII Retaliation) is addressed in Instructions 2-6, Count II (Ohio Whistleblower Protection Act) in Instructions 7-9, and Count IV (Breach of Implied Contract) in Instruction 10. Damages instructions follow but are also organized by claim type where relevant. The special verdict form is similarly divided into Parts I, II, and III corresponding to each claim. The preliminary statement explicitly identifies the three claims and notes that instructions separately address each. This satisfies the criterion of claim-by-claim organization consistent with the standing order.

criteria_results.title: Punitive damages instruction included for Title VII claim
criteria_results.reasoning: Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 16 is explicitly titled 'Punitive Damages --- Title VII Claim Only; Good-Faith Compliance' and explains the standard for awarding punitive damages under Title VII, including the malice or reckless indifference standard from Kolstad, the managerial employee requirement, and the good-faith compliance defense. The special verdict form also includes Questions 5-7 addressing punitive damages for the Title VII claim. The criterion is clearly satisfied.

criteria_results.title: Special verdict form includes separate damages questions per claim
criteria_results.reasoning: The special verdict form clearly separates damages questions by claim. Part I (Title VII) has Questions 2(a) and 2(b) for lost wages/benefits and emotional distress respectively. Part II (Ohio Whistleblower) has Question 10(a) and 10(b) for the same categories. Part III (Implied Contract) has Question 15 for economic damages. Each claim has its own distinct damages questions, not a single combined figure.

criteria_results.title: Mitigation instruction references case-specific factual considerations
criteria_results.reasoning: The mitigation instruction (Proposed Instruction No. 13) explicitly references the Archer-Lawson job offer in the drafting note, and more importantly, the instruction itself is structured around two options: (a) substantially equivalent employment was available and plaintiff failed to seek it, and (b) plaintiff was offered a substantially equivalent position and unreasonably refused it. The drafting note makes clear that option (b) is specifically tied to the December 2023 Archer-Lawson offer ($89,000; industrial coatings; comparable account-management duties; Cleveland area) versus her $97,200 salary. The instruction's structure and the drafting note's factual references (specific job offer, salary comparison, timing of the Aug.–Nov. 2023 gap) constitute case-specific factual considerations. The instruction itself references the framework that applies to a specific refused offer scenario, and the drafting note (which is part of the work product) explicitly ties it to the Archer-Lawson offer. This satisfies the criterion of referencing at least one factual consideration specific to this case.

criteria_results.title: Proposed jury instructions document produced
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced a detailed proposed jury instructions document (proposed-jury-instructions.docx) containing 16 numbered jury instructions covering all three claims (Title VII retaliation, Ohio Whistleblower Protection Act, and implied contract), plus a special verdict form with questions organized by claim. The document clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Cover memorandum produced as separate deliverable
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent produced two clearly separate documents: 'proposed-jury-instructions.docx' containing the jury instructions and special verdict form, and 'instruction-cover-memo.docx' containing the cover memorandum. The cover memo is a distinct deliverable with its own header (KENNERLY, SHAW & BRADDOCK LLP MEMORANDUM), TO/FROM/DATE/RE fields, and substantive content analyzing problems with the pretrial brief instructions. It is clearly distinguishable from the jury instructions document.

criteria_results.title: Instructions advance at least two identifiable defense positions
criteria_results.reasoning: The instructions incorporate all six of the listed defense-favorable positions: (a) but-for causation for Title VII (Instructions 2-3), (b) RIF as legitimate non-retaliatory reason (Instruction 5), (c) internal-reporting prerequisite for Ohio Whistleblower claim (Instructions 7-8), (d) failure to mitigate (Instruction 13), (e) after-acquired evidence doctrine (Instruction 14), and (f) Kolstad good-faith defense to punitive damages (Instruction 16). Each position is legally accurate, citing controlling authority such as Nassar for but-for causation, Ohio Rev. Code § 4113.52 for internal reporting, Ford Motor Co. v. EEOC and Rasimas for mitigation, McKennon for after-acquired evidence, and Kolstad for the good-faith defense. The criterion requires at least two identifiable defense positions, and the output clearly satisfies this with six well-grounded positions.

criteria_results.title: Emotional distress / compensatory damages instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: Instruction No. 15 is explicitly titled 'Compensatory Damages --- Emotional Distress; Pre-Existing Condition' and applies to the Title VII claim (and potentially the Ohio Whistleblower claim). It addresses what the jury may consider: emotional pain, suffering, inconvenience, mental anguish, loss of enjoyment of life, and reasonable medical expenses caused by the termination. It also addresses the pre-existing condition/aggravation issue. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: Back pay instruction included
criteria_results.reasoning: Defendant's Proposed Instruction No. 12 is explicitly titled 'Lost Wages and Benefits (Back Pay)' and provides detailed guidance on calculating lost wages from the termination date through verdict, deductions for interim earnings, inclusion of bonuses and benefits, and exclusion of future lost earnings. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: No hostile-work-environment instruction included (claim was dismissed)
criteria_results.reasoning: The agent's output does not include any jury instruction for a hostile-work-environment claim. The preliminary statement explicitly notes that Count III (hostile work environment) was dismissed with prejudice, and no instruction on that claim appears anywhere in the proposed instructions. References to the dismissed claim appear only to note its dismissal (e.g., in Instruction No. 15's last paragraph, which instructs jurors not to award emotional-distress damages based on the dismissed claim). The criterion requires that no hostile-work-environment instruction be included, and none is.
